newsitem.title: UK: Options - Aluminium call buying dominates LME.
newsitem.headline: Options - Aluminium call buying dominates LME.

text.p: Forward upside aluminium call buying has dominated the London Metal Exchange (LME) options market over the last fortnight, prompted by a sharp rally in prices.
The buying came from all sides of the market, and volatilities moved higher in response, option traders said.
"The buying we saw in the last two weeks was mostly upside aluminium calls for a spread of forward months," said one.
"The market got itself into thinking that prices were not going to pick up, and suddenly they did," another added.
Three month aluminium futures rallied from a 2-1/2 year low of $1,305 a tonne on October 10 to a high of $1,441 on Friday and Monday. It has since retraced to just over $1,400.
Traders said the call buying had dwindled early this week as the market retreated from the highs, but some were still seeing good enquiries.
"Yesterday we were selling calls in good tonnage," said one.
The calls ranged mainly between $1,600 and $1,800 strikes for the latter part of 1997 and first half of 1998.
Volatilities for next year traded as high as 21.50 percent, although they have eased slightly to around 20.50.
Traders said there is a "smile" on volatilities in 1997, with upside calls quoted at slightly higher numbers than at-the-money options.
Buyers were mixed, with traders variously sourcing the buying to consumers, producers and speculators. Some consumers financed calls by selling at-the-money puts, traders said.
The granting came both from the market makers and outside, possibly from Japan, traders said.
Market makers were likely to be generally short of upside forward aluminium calls, leaving some exposed if prices did put on a sustained rally, traders said.
"Some dealers have bought at-the-money forward strikes to cover the volatility exposure, but they still have the risk if the market moves much higher," said one.
Managers at some companies are understood to be watching this exposure carefully in the wake of heavy losses in copper options many suffered as prices crashed in June.
Nearby aluminium volatilities also rose in reaction to rallying futures, although they too were easing from highs.
The copper options market has been quieter, with covering of nearby upside calls the dominant feature.
"People were short of $2,050 and $2,000 calls nearby and have been closing these out by buying back," a trader said.
Some dealers believed exposure on upside calls was smaller than it was in September, when futures spiked on covering against short option positions.
But the risk of another options-driven rally at declaration next Wednesday remained, others argued.
"The short risk is at $2,050 and $2,100 ahead of declaration, and we are not that far away," he said.
Lead volatilities have fallen during the last few days, prompted by fairly active selling of at-the-money doubles in 1997 late last week.
Zinc volatilities moved in the opposite direction, picking up late last week and early this week in reaction to the sharp rise in futures.
December volatility moved to 15.50 percent early on Tuesday from around 14 percent a week ago. Call buying at $1,100 was also noted for the first half of 1997.
"Around 15 percent volatility is historically an area where you should be looking to buy anyway," a trader said.
Tin and nickel options were slow.
